claim: Chromosomal instability (CIN) is persistent chromosome gain or loss through abnormal mitotic segregation.
source: Chromosomal instability (CIN)—persistent chromosome gain or loss through abnormal mitotic segregation—is a hallmark of cancer that drives aneuploidy.
evidence: This is a definitional statement provided in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: CIN is a hallmark of cancer that drives aneuploidy.
source: Chromosomal instability (CIN)—persistent chromosome gain or loss through abnormal mitotic segregation—is a hallmark of cancer that drives aneuploidy.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific understanding referenced in the manuscript.

claim: Intrinsic chromosome mis-segregation rate can inform prognosis.
source: Intrinsic chromosome mis-segregation rate, a measure of CIN, can inform prognosis and is a promising biomarker for response to anti-microtubule agents.
evidence: This claim is based on the potential clinical utility discussed in the abstract.

claim: Intrinsic chromosome mis-segregation rate is a promising biomarker for response to anti-microtubule agents.
source: Intrinsic chromosome mis-segregation rate, a measure of CIN, can inform prognosis and is a promising biomarker for response to anti-microtubule agents.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the potential application of CIN measurement.

claim: Existing methodologies to measure chromosome mis-segregation rate are labor intensive, indirect, and confounded by selection against aneuploid cells.
source: However, existing methodologies to measure this rate are labor intensive, indirect, and confounded by selection against aneuploid cells, which reduces observable diversity.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of current methods provided in the abstract.

claim: Selection against aneuploid cells reduces observable diversity.
source: However, existing methodologies to measure this rate are labor intensive, indirect, and confounded by selection against aneuploid cells, which reduces observable diversity.
evidence: This is an inference about the biological effect of selection on observable karyotype diversity.

claim: The authors developed a framework to measure CIN accounting for karyotype selection using simulations with various levels of CIN and models of selection.
source: We developed a framework to measure CIN, accounting for karyotype selection, using simulations with various levels of CIN and models of selection.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach taken in the study.

claim: Approximate Bayesian computation was used to infer mis-segregation rates and karyotype selection from single-cell sequencing data.
source: To identify the model parameters that best fit karyotype data from single-cell sequencing, we used approximate Bayesian computation to infer mis-segregation rates and karyotype selection.
evidence: This describes the computational method used for parameter inference.

claim: Paclitaxel causes extensive chromosome mis-segregation at a rate of 18.5 ± 0.5 per division.
source: Experimental validation confirmed the extensive chromosome mis-segregation rates caused by the chemotherapy paclitaxel (18.5 ± 0.5/division).
evidence: This is an experimental finding reported in the abstract with quantitative data.

claim: Inferred mis-segregation rates in clinical samples fell within direct observations of cancer cell lines.
source: Extending this approach to clinical samples revealed that inferred rates fell within direct observations of cancer cell lines.
evidence: This is a validation of the method by comparing inferred rates to observed rates.

claim: CIN is characterized by persistent whole-chromosome gain and loss through mis-segregation during cell division.
source: Chromosomal instability (CIN) is characterized by persistent whole-chromosome gain and loss through mis-segregation during cell division.
evidence: This is a definitional statement in the introduction.

claim: Genome instability is a hallmark of cancer.
source: Genome instability is a hallmark of cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a foundational cancer biology paper.

claim: CIN is the principal driver of aneuploidy.
source: one type, CIN, is the principal driver of aneuploidy, a feature of ~80% of solid tumors (Hancock et al., 2004; Knouse et al., 2017; Weaver and Cleveland, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations indicating the prevalence of aneuploidy in tumors.

claim: Aneuploidy is a feature of approximately 80% of solid tumors.
source: one type, CIN, is the principal driver of aneuploidy, a feature of ~80% of solid tumors (Hancock et al., 2004; Knouse et al., 2017; Weaver and Cleveland, 2006).
evidence: This statistic is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: CIN potentiates tumorigenesis.
source: CIN potentiates tumorigenesis (Foijer et al., 2017; Levine et al., 2017; Silk et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating the role of CIN in tumor development.

claim: CIN associates with therapeutic resistance.
source: and associates with therapeutic resistance (Ippolito et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2011; Lukow et al., 2020; Pavelka et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations linking CIN to resistance to therapy.

claim: CIN associates with metastasis.
source: metastasis (Bakhoum et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on CIN and metastasis.

claim: CIN associates with poor survival outcomes.
source: and poor survival outcomes (Bakhoum et al., 2011; Denu et al., 2016; Jamal-Hanjani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: CIN has not emerged as a clinical biomarker in part because it is challenging to quantify.
source: Despite its importance, CIN has not emerged as a clinical biomarker, in part because it is challenging to quantify.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of the field.

claim: Clinical outcomes partially depend on aneuploidy of specific chromosomes.
source: For example, clinical outcomes partially depend on aneuploidy of specific chromosomes (Davoli et al., 2013; Sheltzer et al., 2017; Vasudevan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies examining chromosome-specific effects.

claim: Higher levels of CIN suppress tumor growth when they surpass a critical threshold.
source: Further, higher levels of CIN suppress tumor growth when they surpass a critical threshold, thought to be due to lethal loss of essential genes and irregular expression due to imbalanced gene dosage (Funk et al., 2021; Silk et al., 2013; Weaver and Cleveland, 2008; Zasadil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and provides a mechanistic explanation.

claim: Baseline CIN may predict chemotherapeutic response to paclitaxel.
source: Moreover, baseline CIN may predict chemotherapeutic response to paclitaxel (Janssen et al., 2009; Swanton et al., 2009)
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: CIN is proposed to both promote detection by or evasion from the immune system.
source: and is proposed to both promote detection by or evasion from the immune system (Davoli et al., 2017; Santaguida et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the dual role of CIN in immune interactions, supported by citations.

claim: No single or standardized analytically valid measure of CIN has emerged.
source: No single or standardized analytically valid measure of CIN has emerged and this gap has precluded its clinical validation as a prognostic or predictive biomarker.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of CIN measurement.

claim: Prior measures of CIN use various means to compare levels in tumors or populations but do not establish a standardized quantitative rate.
source: Prior measures of CIN use various means to compare levels in tumors or populations, but do not establish a standardized quantitative rate.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of existing methods.

claim: FISH and mitotic visualization approaches are laborious.
source: FISH and mitotic visualization approaches are laborious.
evidence: This is a practical limitation of existing methods.

claim: Direct visualization of mitotic defects to measure CIN is only possible in the most proliferative tumors.
source: Direct visualization of mitotic defects to measure CIN is only possible in the most proliferative tumors where enough cells are captured in short-lived mitosis.
evidence: This is a limitation based on the biology of mitosis.

claim: FISH typically quantifies only a subset of chromosomes, which will be misleading if there is bias toward specific chromosome gains/losses.
source: FISH typically quantifies only a subset of chromosomes, which will be misleading if there is bias toward specific chromosome gains/losses (Dumont et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological limitation supported by a citation.

claim: Gene expression scores are not specific to CIN and correlate highly with proliferation and structural aneuploidy.
source: While gene expression scores are proposed as indirect measures of CIN, they are not specific to CIN and correlate highly with proliferation and structural aneuploidy (Carter et al., 2006; Sheltzer, 2013).
evidence: This is a critique of gene expression-based CIN measures supported by citations.

claim: Single-cell sequencing promises major advances in quantitative measures of CIN by displaying cell-cell variation for each chromosome across hundreds of cells.
source: Single-cell sequencing promises major advances in quantitative measures of CIN by displaying cell-cell variation for each chromosome across hundreds of cells (Navin et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the potential of single-cell sequencing, supported by citations.

claim: Single-cell analyses have identified surprisingly low cell-cell karyotype variation, even when mitotic errors are directly observed by microscopy.
source: To date, single-cell analyses have identified surprisingly low cell-cell karyotype variation, even when mitotic errors are directly observed by microscopy (Bolhaqueiro et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2018; Nelson et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This observation is supported by multiple citations to single-cell sequencing studies.

claim: Selection reduces karyotype variance in cancer cell populations that directly exhibit mitotic errors.
source: Indeed, selection reduces karyotype variance in cancer cell populations that directly exhibit mitotic errors (Gerstung et al., 2020; Ippolito et al., 2020; Lukow et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating the effect of selection.

claim: The authors built their framework on the use of phylogenetic topology measures to quantify underlying evolutionary processes.
source: We built our framework on the use of phylogenetic topology measures to quantify underlying evolutionary processes (Mooers and Heard, 1997); in this case to quantify CIN from both the diversity and the aneuploid phylogeny within a tumor.
evidence: This describes the conceptual basis of the method, supported by a citation.

claim: The authors used an agent-based model of CIN to determine how distinct types and degrees of selective pressure shape the karyotype distribution and population structure of tumor cells.
source: Using an agent-based model of CIN, we determine how distinct types and degrees of selective pressure shape the karyotype distribution and population structure of tumor cells at different rates of chromosome mis-segregation.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: The authors applied their model to quantify CIN caused by paclitaxel in culture.
source: We apply this model to quantify CIN caused by the chemotherapeutic paclitaxel in culture.
evidence: This describes an experimental application of the model.

claim: The authors measured CIN in cancer biopsy and organoid samples using existing single-cell whole-genome sequencing data.
source: Next, using existing single-cell whole-genome sequencing data (scDNAseq), we measure CIN in cancer biopsy and organoid samples.
evidence: This describes the application of the method to clinical samples.

claim: The Gene Abundance model assumes cellular fitness declines as the cell's karyotype diverges from a balanced euploid karyotype.
source: The Gene Abundance model is based on the relatively low incidence of aneuploidy in normal tissues and assumes cellular fitness declines as the cell's karyotype diverges from a balanced euploid karyotype (Sheltzer and Amon, 2011; Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes one of the selection models used, supported by citations.

claim: In the Gene Abundance model, a chromosome's contribution to cellular fitness is weighted by its abundance of genes.
source: When an individual chromosome diverges from euploid balance (2 N, 3 N, 4 N, for example), its contribution to cellular fitness is weighted by its abundance of genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, left).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the Gene Abundance model, with reference to a figure.

claim: The Driver Density model assumes that each chromosome's contribution to cellular fitness is weighted by its ratio of Tumor suppressor genes, Oncogenes, and Essential genes.
source: Alternatively, the Driver Density model assumes that each chromosome's contribution to cellular fitness is weighted by its ratio of Tumor suppressor genes, Oncogenes, and Essential genes (TOEs)(Davoli et al., 2013; Laughney et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes another selection model, supported by citations.

claim: Driver Density selection favors loss of chromosomes with many tumor suppressors and favors gain of chromosomes replete with oncogenes and essential genes.
source: For example, Driver Density selection will favor loss of chromosomes with many tumor suppressors and favor gain of chromosomes replete with oncogenes and essential genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, right).
evidence: This describes the expected outcomes of the Driver Density model, with reference to a figure.

claim: The hybrid averaged model accounts for both karyotypic balance and TOE densities.
source: The hybrid averaged model accounts for both karyotypic balance and TOE densities (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, middle).
evidence: This describes a third selection model that combines features of the other two.

claim: Simulations started with 100 euploid cells.
source: Briefly, simulations started with 100 euploid cells and were run in discrete time steps with variable rates of selective pressure, S, and rates of chromosome mis-segregation (Pmisseg, see definitions in Table 2).
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the simulations.

claim: During each time step, cells have a Pdivision (= 0.5 for euploid) chance of dividing.
source: During each time step, cells have a Pdivision ( = 0.5 for euploid) chance of dividing.
evidence: This is a parameter of the simulation model.

claim: Each dividing cell has a Pmisseg chance of improper segregation of each chromosome.
source: Each dividing cell has a Pmisseg chance of improper segregation of each chromosome.
evidence: This is a key parameter defining CIN in the model.

claim: Cells are removed from the population if any given chromosome has copy number 0 or >6.
source: Cells are removed from the population if any given chromosome has copy number 0 or >6.
evidence: This is a constraint in the simulation model.

claim: Pseudo-Moran or Wright-Fisher models are employed to limit the modeled cell population.
source: Due to computational limitations, pseudo-Moran or Wright-Fisher models are employed to limit the modeled cell population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This describes a computational strategy used in the simulations.

claim: Population limits did not significantly affect the measures extracted from simulated populations.
source: These limits did not significantly affect the measures extracted from these populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a validation of the modeling approach, supported by a figure.

claim: The simulated cell number increases rapidly to the pseudo-Moran cap of 3000, where it remains.
source: As expected, the simulated cell number increases rapidly to the pseudo-Moran cap of 3000, where it remains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations, shown in a figure.

claim: Diversity of the cell population, expressed as mean karyotypic variance, increases over time and depends on mis-segregation rate and selection levels.
source: As displayed in Figure 2B, diversity of the cell population, expressed as mean karyotypic variance increases over time, but also depends on mis-segregation rate, and selection levels (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a key finding from the simulations, illustrated in a figure.

claim: High mis-segregation rates and low selection enhance the variance of the population.
source: As expected, high mis-segregation rates (Pmisseg, Y axis) and low selection (S = 0; top row) enhance the variance of the population.
evidence: This is an expected outcome from the model parameters.

claim: Without selection (S = 0), all models returned comparable profiles over time, resembling neutral selection.
source: Further, without selection (S = 0; top row) all models returned comparable profiles over time, resembling neutral selection.
evidence: This is an observation about model behavior under neutral conditions.

claim: When selective pressure is applied (S > 0), distinct profiles appear for different selection models.
source: However, when selective pressure is applied (S > 0), the distinct profiles appear.
evidence: This shows that selection models produce different outcomes.

claim: The Abundance model negatively selects against all aneuploid karyotypes and yields low heterogeneity that increases modestly with mis-segregation rate.
source: The abundance model (first column) negatively selects against all aneuploid karyotypes and yields low heterogeneity that increases modestly with mis-segregation rate.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the Abundance model in simulations.

claim: With the Driver model, there is a sharp increase in heterogeneity even at low mis-segregation rates.
source: With the Driver model (second column), there is a sharp increase in heterogeneity even at low mis-segregation rates, as this model favors specific aneuploid states that maximizes oncogenes and minimizes tumor suppressors.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the Driver model in simulations.

claim: The Hybrid model falls between the Abundance and Driver models in terms of heterogeneity.
source: The Hybrid model falls between the other two.
evidence: This describes the intermediate behavior of the Hybrid model.

claim: Results were not specific to the pseudo-Moran process of capping at 3000 cells—dynamics were similar in the constant-population Wright-Fisher model.
source: Results were not specific to the pseudo-Moran process of capping at 3000 cells—dynamics were similar in the constant-population Wright-Fisher model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a validation showing robustness of findings across different population models.

claim: In many cases, the mean ploidy of the populations tend to increase over time.
source: In many cases, the mean ploidy of the populations tend to increase over time (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), particularly in the absence of selection (S = 0; top).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations shown in figures.

claim: The tendency for ploidy to increase is likely due to a higher permissiveness to chromosome gains than losses in the model.
source: This is likely due to a higher permissiveness to chromosome gains than losses in our model (since cells 'die' with nullisomy or any chromosome >6, the optimum is 3.0).
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the observed ploidy increase based on model constraints.

claim: With selection (S = 10; S = 100), the models diverge in their ploidy dynamics.
source: With selection (S = 10; S = 100 rows), the models diverge.
evidence: This describes differential behavior of models under selection.

claim: In the Abundance model, populations remain near diploid under selection.
source: In the abundance model, populations remain near diploid.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the Abundance model under selection.

claim: With the Driver model, the average ploidy increases more rapidly due to favoring aneuploidy states that favor high oncogenes and low tumor suppressors.
source: With the Driver model, the average ploidy increases more rapidly due to favoring aneuploidy states that favor high oncogenes and low tumor suppressors, consistent with previous computational models built on chromosome-specific driver densities (Davoli et al., 2013; Laughney et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the Driver model behavior and is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: Under the Hybrid model, ploidy increases modestly.
source: Under the Hybrid model, ploidy increases modestly.
evidence: This describes the intermediate behavior of the Hybrid model.

claim: Genome doubling occurs early in tumor initiation relative to other copy number changes in some tumors.
source: In some tumors, genome doubling occurs early in tumor initiation relative to other copy number changes (Bielski et al., 2018; Gerstung et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on genome doubling in cancer.

claim: Genome doubling buffers against loss of chromosomes and thereby favors aneuploidy.
source: Genome doubling buffers against loss of chromosomes and thereby favors aneuploidy.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of genome doubling on aneuploidy tolerance.

claim: Both diploids and tetraploids tend to converge toward the near-triploid state (ploidy ~3), as observed in many human cancers.
source: Both diploids and tetraploids tend to converge toward the near-triploid state (ploidy ~3), as observed in many human cancers (Carter et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations that is consistent with observations in human cancers, supported by a citation.

claim: Tetraploidy buffered against the negative effects of cellular fitness in the Abundance model compared with diploid cells.
source: Compared with diploid cells, tetraploidy buffered against the negative effects of cellular fitness in the Abundance model, despite generating similar levels of diversity over time (Figure 2F and G)
evidence: This is a finding from comparing diploid and tetraploid simulations, shown in figures.

claim: Tetraploidy serves as an intermediate enabling a near-triploid karyotype that is common in many cancers.
source: This is consistent with the idea that tetraploidy serves as an intermediate enabling a near-triploid karyotype that is common in many cancers (Bielski et al., 2018; López et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation consistent with cited literature.

claim: In the Driver model, tetraploidy did not provide a selective advantage to high-CIN tumors.
source: By contrast, in the Driver model, tetraploidy did not provide a selective advantage to high-CIN tumors (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations shown in a figure.

claim: The agent-based model recapitulates expected key aspects of tumor evolution.
source: Taken together, the agent-based model recapitulates expected key aspects of tumor evolution, lending credence to our model.
evidence: This is an assessment of the model's validity based on its ability to reproduce known phenomena.

claim: Selection pressure profoundly shapes karyotype diversity.
source: Yet, our model suggests that selection pressure will profoundly shape this diversity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Population diversity is limited under the Abundance model.
source: As expected, population diversity is limited under the Abundance model (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from long-term simulations shown in a figure.

claim: After 3000 time steps under the Abundance model, only a small number of unique alterations and sub-clonal alterations existed.
source: Even after 3000 time steps, only a small number of unique alterations and sub-clonal alterations ( + 13 p/–15 p/–22 p) existed, likely passenger alterations as they offer no fitness advantage in this model.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations with an interpretation about passenger alterations.

claim: The karyotype average of 1500 cells across five replicates under the Abundance model resembled a diploid karyotype.
source: Moreover, the karyotype average of 1500 cells across five replicates resembled a diploid karyotype (Figure 3C, row 1), indicating that the Abundance model provides stabilizing selection around the euploid karyotype.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations shown in a figure, with an interpretation about stabilizing selection.

claim: Populations simulated under the Abundance model with elevated selection (S = 25) quickly reach a low, steady-state level of karyotype diversity and fitness.
source: In fact, populations simulated under this model with elevated selection (S = 25) quickly reach a low, steady-state level of karyotype diversity and fitness while those with the unmodified selection values (S = 1) take a longer time to reach this steady-state and have similar levels of karyotype diversity and fitness as the other models (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the dynamics of reaching steady state under different selection strengths, shown in a figure.

claim: The steady state under the Abundance model is consistent for tetraploid cells as well as when the upper ploidy constraint is eased.
source: We found this steady state to be consistent for tetraploid cells as well as when we eased the upper ploidy constraint from nc c = 6 to an extreme nc c = 10, when we imposed a severe, 90% fitness reduction for all cells with a haploidy, and when we simulated populations under the Wright-Fisher model (Figure 3C, rows 2–4).
evidence: This is a robustness check showing consistency across different model variations, shown in a figure.

claim: The Driver Density and Hybrid models generate much more diversity than the Abundance model.
source: The Driver Density and Hybrid models generate much more diversity (Figure 3B) but nevertheless converge by 3,000 timesteps (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison of model behaviors shown in figures.

claim: Without selection (neutral model), there is high diversity and no convergence over time.
source: Without selection (neutral model), there is high diversity and no convergence over time.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the neutral model.

claim: Long-term populations are strongly shaped by the model of karyotype selection for a given Pmisseg.
source: Taken together, long-term populations are strongly shaped by the model of karyotype selection for a given Pmisseg, but relatively insensitive to other particular features of the model.
evidence: This is a conclusion about which model features are most important.

claim: Phylogenetic trees provide insights into evolutionary processes of genetic diversification and selection.
source: Phylogenetic trees provide insights into evolutionary processes of genetic diversification and selection.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The topology of the phylogenetic tree has been used as a quantitative measure of the underlying evolutionary processes.
source: Moreover, the topology of the phylogenetic tree has been used as a quantitative measure of the underlying evolutionary processes (Colijn and Plazzotta, 2018; Dayarian and Shraiman, 2014; Manceau et al., 2015; Neher et al., 2014; Scott et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using phylogenetic topology.

claim: Aneuploidy and mean karyotypic variance (MKV) decrease with selective pressure, a trend that is robust at high mis-segregation rates.
source: As seen previously, aneuploidy and mean karyotypic variance (MKV) decrease with selective pressure, a trend that is robust at high mis-segregation rates (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of phylogenetic measures, shown in a figure.

claim: Colless indices increase with mis-segregation rates and selective pressures.
source: By contrast, Colless indices increase with mis-segregation rates and selective pressures, as the resulting variation and selection generate phylogenetic asymmetry.
evidence: This describes the relationship between Colless index and model parameters.

claim: Cherries decrease with selection due to selection against many aneuploidies.
source: Cherries, by contrast, decrease with selection due to selection against many aneuploidies (Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes the relationship between cherries and selection, shown in a figure.

claim: Four phylogenetic parameters can retain information about chromosome mis-segregation: aneuploidy, MKV, Colless, and Cherries.
source: Therefore, we tentatively selected 4 phylogenetic parameters that can retain information about chromosome missegregation—aneuploidy, MKV, Colless, and Cherries.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the analysis.

claim: When considering heterogeneity alone, simulations performed under high CIN/high selection and low CIN/low selection associate closely.
source: This analysis indicates that when considering heterogeneity alone simulations performed under high CIN/high selection (yellow) and low CIN/low selection (red) associate closely, meaning these measures of heterogeneity are not sufficient to distinguish these disparate conditions (Figure 4E, left).
evidence: This is a finding from dimensionality reduction analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Combining measures of heterogeneity with those of phylogenetic topology can discriminate between simulations with disparate levels of CIN and selection.
source: By contrast, combining measures of heterogeneity with those of phylogenetic topology can discriminate between simulations with disparate levels of CIN and selection (Figure 4E, right).
evidence: This is a key finding showing the value of phylogenetic topology, shown in a figure.

claim: Phylogenetic topology preserves information about underlying levels of selective pressure and rates of chromosome mis-segregation.
source: Together these results indicate that phylogenetic topology preserves information about underlying levels of selective pressure and rates of chromosome mis-segregation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis.

claim: Treatment with 20 nM paclitaxel generates widespread aneuploidy due to chromosome mis-segregation on multipolar mitotic spindles.
source: We treated CAL51 breast cancer cells with either a DMSO control or 20 nM paclitaxel, which generates widespread aneuploidy due to chromosome mis-segregation on multipolar mitotic spindles (Zasadil et al., 2014), verified in this experiment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by a citation and verified in the current study, shown in a figure.

claim: At 48 hr, cells will have undergone 1–2 mitoses.
source: At 48 hr cells will have undergone 1–2 mitoses and, consistent with abnormal chromosome segregation, we observe broadened DNA content distributions by flow cytometry (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference about cell division timing supported by flow cytometry data shown in a figure.

claim: Virtually all cells had extensive aneuploidy after paclitaxel treatment.
source: As expected, virtually all cells had extensive aneuploidy after paclitaxel, in contrast with low variance in the control (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in a figure.

claim: The mean of the resultant aneuploid karyotypes for each chromosome still resembled those of bulk-sequenced cells.
source: Additionally, the mean of the resultant aneuploid karyotypes for each chromosome still resembled those of bulk-sequenced cells, highlighting that bulk-sequencing is an ensemble average, and does not detect variation in population aneuploidy, particularly with balanced mis-segregation events (Figure 5B, single-cell mean and bulk).
evidence: This is a comparison between single-cell and bulk sequencing shown in a figure, with an interpretation about the limitations of bulk sequencing.

claim: Cells exposed to 20 nM paclitaxel mis-segregate 18.5 ± 0.5 chromosomes, assuming a single mitosis.
source: In quantifying the absolute deviation from the modal control karyotype in each cell, and assuming a single mitosis, cells exposed to 20 nM paclitaxel mis-segregate 18.5 ± 0.5—a Pmisseg of ~0.42 considering the control's sub-diploid modal karyotype (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: The majority of mis-segregations in paclitaxel-treated cells appeared to be whole-chromosome mis-segregations.
source: The majority of these appeared to be whole-chromosome mis-segregations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in a figure.

claim: The experimental data from paclitaxel-treated cells mapped to simulations using high mis-segregation rates and relatively low selection.
source: The experimental data mapped to those from simulations using high mis-segregation rates and relatively low selection (red point, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental and simulated data shown in a figure.

claim: ABC inferred a chromosome mis-segregation rate of 0.396 ± 0.003 (or 17.4 ± 0.1 chromosomes) for paclitaxel-treated cells.
source: In doing so, this analysis inferred a chromosome mis-segregation rate of 0.396 ± 0.003 (or 17.4 ± 0.1 chromosomes; mean ± SE), which compares favorably with the experimentally observed rate of 18.5 ± 0.5 (Figure 5E; dashed line represents experimental rate, white '+' the inferred rate).
evidence: This is the result of ABC inference compared to the experimental measurement, shown in a figure.

claim: The distribution of accepted values for selection in paclitaxel-treated cells was skewed toward lower pressure (21 ± 0.4).
source: The distribution of accepted values for selection was skewed toward lower pressure (21 ± 0.4; mean ± SE), meaning that karyotype selection had little bearing on the result at this time point, consistent with the absence of selection in a 48-hr experiment.
evidence: This is a result from ABC inference with an interpretation about the short experimental timeframe.

claim: The incidence of nullisomy in the simulated population was higher than in the paclitaxel-treated populations at the observed mis-segregation rate.
source: Interestingly, the incidence of nullisomy in the simulated population was higher than in the paclitaxel-treated populations at the observed mis-segregation rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a comparison between simulated and experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: The difference in nullisomy incidence could be due to spindle pole clustering, a recovery mechanism often seen in paclitaxel-treated cells that causes non-random chromosome mis-segregations.
source: This could be due to spindle pole clustering, a recovery mechanism often seen in paclitaxel-treated cells that causes non-random chromosome mis-segregations.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed discrepancy.

claim: Even small sample sizes can accurately infer the mis-segregation rate in the paclitaxel context, with a low standard error.
source: We found that even small sample sizes can accurately infer the mis-segregation rate, in this context, with a low standard error (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B-D).
evidence: This is a finding from the sample size analysis shown in figures.

claim: A sample size of 60 cells produced the most accurate measurement at 99.5% accuracy and a standard error of 0.008 (±0.35 chromosomes) for paclitaxel-treated cells.
source: A sample size of 60 cells produced the most accurate measurement at 99.5% and a standard error of 0.008 ( ± 0.35 chromosomes).
evidence: This is a specific finding about optimal sample size for the paclitaxel experiment.

claim: Across all mis-segregation rates and selective pressures in simulations, random samples of 200 cells had a median percent accuracy of 90% and median standard error of 0.0003 (±0.0138 chromosomes per division).
source: Across all mis-segregation rates and selective pressures, random samples of 200 cells had a median percent accuracy of 90% and median standard error of 0.0003 ( ± 0.0138 chromosomes per division).
evidence: This is a finding from the sample size analysis using simulated data.

claim: The authors recommend using 200 cells from a single sampled site, which provides ≥90% accuracy at biologically relevant time scales and rates of mis-segregation.
source: In conclusion, we recommend using 200 cells from a single sampled site which, at biologically relevant time scales and rates of mis-segregation, provides ≥90% accuracy.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the analysis.

claim: The Abundance model resulted in simulated data that best resembled experimental data from tumor samples and organoids.
source: With these model parameters chosen, we evaluated the different selection models, and found that the Abundance model resulted in simulated data that best resembled experimental data, for both exponential and constant-population dynamics (Table 3).
evidence: This is a result from model selection analysis shown in a table.

claim: ABC analysis inferred rates of chromosome mis-segregation in tumor samples and organoids to be about 0.001–0.006.
source: With ABC, inferred parameters fall within rates of mis-segregation of about 0.001–0.006.
evidence: This is a summary of the ABC inference results for clinical samples.

claim: Inferred rates of 0.001–0.006 translate to a range of about 5–38% of cell divisions having one chromosome mis-segregation when applied to a near-diploid cell.
source: Applied to a near-diploid cell, this translates to a range of about 5–38% of cell divisions having one chromosome mis-segregation.
evidence: This is a conversion of the inferred rates to a more interpretable metric.

claim: Inferred rates of chromosome mis-segregation in tumor samples fall within the range of approximated per chromosome rates experimentally observed in cancer cell lines and human tumors.
source: Importantly, these inferred rates of chromosome mis-segregation fall within the range of approximated per chromosome rates experimentally observed in cancer cell lines and human tumors (Figure 6E;Table 4, Table 5; Bakhoum et al., 2014; Bakhoum et al., 2011; Bakhoum et al., 2009; Dewhurst et al., 2014; Nicholson et al., 2015; Orr et al., 2016; Thompson and Compton, 2008; Worrall et al., 2018; Zasadil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a validation of the inferred rates by comparison to published data, shown in a figure and tables.

claim: Higher inferred mis-segregation rates tended to coincide with lower inferred selection in tumor samples.
source: Higher inferred mis-segregation rates tended to coincide with lower inferred selection experienced in these samples (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an observation about the relationship between inferred parameters, shown in a figure.

claim: Posterior distributions in tumor samples were skewed toward high selection (S) indicating the presence of stabilizing selection in all cases.
source: Posterior distributions in these samples were skewed toward high selection (S) indicating the presence stabilizing selection in all cases, where the average of the distributions of some samples were slightly lower or higher (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the posterior distributions shown in a figure.

claim: There was a strong correlation between inferred mis-segregation rates from CRC PDOs and those directly measured in live imaging.
source: There was a strong correlation but for two outliers—14T and U1T (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a validation of the method by comparing inferred rates to direct observations, shown in a figure.

claim: When adjusting to the same scale and correcting for cell ploidy, inferred and observed mis-segregation rates follow a strong positive linear trend with a slightly lower slope than a 1:1 correlation.
source: In fact, when adjusting to the same scale and correcting for cell ploidy, these data follow a strong positive linear trend with a slightly lower slope than a 1:1 correlation, which could reflect an overestimation of mis-segregation rates in the microscopy data (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is an analysis of the relationship between inferred and observed rates shown in a figure, with an interpretation about potential overestimation in microscopy.

claim: Single-cell DNA sequencing now promises detailed karyotypic analysis across hundreds of cells.
source: Single-cell DNA sequencing now promises detailed karyotypic analysis across hundreds of cells, yet selective pressure suppresses the observed karyotype heterogeneity within a tumor.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential and limitations of scDNAseq.

claim: Optimal clinical measurement of CIN may be achieved with scDNAseq, but must additionally account for selective pressure.
source: Optimal clinical measurement of CIN may be achieved with scDNAseq, but must additionally account for selective pressure, which reduces karyotype heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the requirements for clinical CIN measurement.

claim: CIN measures appear to predict therapeutic response to paclitaxel.
source: For example, CIN measures appear to predict therapeutic response to paclitaxel (Janssen et al., 2009; Scribano et al., 2021; Swanton et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on CIN and paclitaxel response.

claim: The authors conclude that scDNAseq is the most complete and tractable measure of cellular karyotypes.
source: We conclude that scDNAseq is the most complete and tractable measure of cellular karyotypes, and sampling at least 200 cells, coupled with computational models and ABC, promises to offer the best measure of tumor CIN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Sampling at least 200 cells, coupled with computational models and ABC, promises to offer the best measure of tumor CIN.
source: We conclude that scDNAseq is the most complete and tractable measure of cellular karyotypes, and sampling at least 200 cells, coupled with computational models and ABC, promises to offer the best measure of tumor CIN.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the study.

claim: This work provides the necessary framework to quantify CIN in human tumors and develop it as a predictive biomarker.
source: This work provides the necessary framework to quantify CIN in human tumors and develop it as a predictive biomarker.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the work.
